back: The series of activities and/or phases a project passes through from its start to its closure.
A collection of logically related project activities that culminates in one or more deliverables and/or outcomes.
A review at the end (or start) of a phase to check exit criteria and make a go/no-go decision. Also called stage gate or gate review.
Entrance: what must be true for a project to move into a phase. Exit: what must be true to complete it.

front: When is risk highest? When is the cost of change highest?
back: Risk and uncertainty: at the start. Cost of change: toward the end.
The means used to create and evolve the product, service or result during the project life cycle: predictive, adaptive or hybrid.
Approach: the method used across the project. Phase: the specific stage where deliverables are built and tested.
Scope, schedule and cost are defined early and planning is done up front. Also called waterfall, plan-driven or traditional.

front: When is a predictive approach best?
back: Clear, stable requirements; high safety or regulatory needs; changes are difficult or costly; large investments.
Requirements are progressively elaborated and changed based on feedback, in timeboxed cycles. Also called change-driven or agile.

front: When is an adaptive approach best?
back: High uncertainty and volatility, innovation, unstable scope, and when frequent feedback adds value.
A combination of predictive and adaptive elements. Most projects today can benefit from it.
Adaptive then predictive rollout; both used together throughout; largely predictive with an adaptive part; largely adaptive with a predictive part.
Iterative: refine and improve through repeated cycles. Incremental: deliver small usable segments that build on each other.
Predictive: scope fixed, budget and schedule vary. Adaptive: budget and schedule fixed, scope varies.
The scope, schedule and cost baselines taken together.
A visual workflow method that limits work in process (WIP), based on lean principles, for continuous delivery without overburdening the team.
Identify and address the most significant limiting factor that stands in the way of achieving a goal.
1 to 4 weeks, with a demonstration of what was accomplished at the end.
Single delivery, multiple deliveries, periodic deliveries, continuous delivery.
Multiple deliveries on a regular, fixed schedule, such as every two weeks. Common in adaptive approaches.

front: Three groups of factors for choosing an approach
back: Deliverables, project, organization.
Method: a systematic series of steps. Tool kit: a collection of tools and techniques to choose from. Disciplined Agile is a tool kit.

front: Recommended team size in some adaptive frameworks
back: Three to nine team members.
